name: Data Version Control
description: Data Version Control (DVC) is an open-source tool that records which version of a dataset or model was used at each point in a machine learning project. It works alongside Git, the standard system for tracking changes to code. DVC keeps large data and model files in separate storage, such as a cloud storage service, and puts a small pointer file into Git that holds a fingerprint (hash) of the file's contents. A team can also describe a pipeline, meaning the ordered steps from raw data through preprocessing to a trained model, and DVC then records fingerprints of each step's inputs, settings and outputs. Committed to Git, these files give a dated history of how data and models changed and let the team restore an earlier version, but only for what was added to DVC and committed.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital research group trains a chest X-ray classifier. When a regulator asks which images and preprocessing produced the version it submitted, the group checks out the tagged Git commit, shows the dataset fingerprints and pipeline steps recorded in it, and restores that exact data to confirm.

A lender's credit-scoring team sees approval rates shift after a quarterly data refresh. Using DVC with Git, they list the files that changed between the datasets behind the last two model releases, trace the shift to one refresh, and decide whether to revert to the earlier data version.

A flood-forecasting agency versions its river-sensor calibration data and the feature-extraction steps that use it. When a forecast is challenged, an independent reviewer can see from the version history who changed the calibration data and when, and which model release was trained on each version.

A manufacturer's quality team retrains a defect-detection model each month and tags each release in Git with the DVC record of its training images. When a customer reports a missed defect, the team retrieves the exact images behind the model then in use and sees what was added or removed since the previous release.

limitations.description: DVC records only what has been added to it and committed to Git. Data edited outside DVC, or changes that were never committed, leave no trace, and nothing in the history shows what is missing, so the record is only as complete as the team's habits.

Lineage exists only for steps defined as DVC pipeline stages. A study of 56 open-source projects found that 85.7% used only DVC's versioning and tracking feature, so a project that uses DVC may hold no record of how its data was preprocessed or its model trained.

Restoring an earlier model takes more than DVC's files. The code, the software environment and the stored data must all still exist, and the pipeline lock file records commands, file fingerprints and parameter values but not library versions, so a restored pipeline can still give different results.

Scale costs time and storage. A changed data file is stored again as a new copy, and the documentation notes that operations such as pulling become slow with tens of thousands of files, pointing teams that need to branch and merge large datasets in object storage to a different tool.
When several people change the same data files or pipeline, merge conflicts in DVC's tracking files have to be resolved by hand. Without agreed branching rules the history becomes hard to trust.

resources.title: On the Co-evolution of ML Pipelines and Source Code - Empirical Study of DVC Projects
resources.abstract: The growing popularity of machine learning (ML) applications has led to the introduction of software engineering tools such as Data Versioning Control (DVC), MLFlow and Pachyderm that enable versioning ML data, models, pipelines and model evaluation metrics. Since these versioned ML artifacts need to be synchronized not only with each other, but also with the source and test code of the software applications into which the models are integrated, prior findings on co-evolution and coupling between software artifacts might need to be revisited. Hence, in order to understand the degree of coupling between ML-related and other software artifacts, as well as the adoption of ML versioning features, this paper empirically studies the usage of DVC in 391 Github projects, 25 of which in detail. Our results show that more than half of the DVC files in a project are changed at least once every one-tenth of the project's lifetime. Furthermore, we observe a tight coupling between DVC files and other artifacts, with 1/4 pull requests changing source code and 1/2 pull requests changing tests requiring a change to DVC files. As additional evidence of the observed complexity associated with adopting ML-related software engineering tools like DVC, an average of 78% of the studied projects showed a non-constant trend in pipeline complexity.

resources.title: DVC in Open Source ML-development: The Action and the Reaction
resources.abstract: Machine Learning (ML) systems are gaining popularity, reshaping various domains ranging from customer services to software engineering. The effectiveness of ML systems is dependent on the quality of their training data. Therefore, practitioners invest substantial time experimenting with different data, parameters, and models to guarantee the quality of the end system. Prior work highlighted unique challenges of developing ML systems, particularly concerning versioning data and models. Recently, various tools such as DVC and MLFlow have emerged to aid developers in the storage and tracking of data. Despite their growing popularity, very little is known about their usage patterns and impact on open-source software (OSS) systems. To address this gap, we conducted an empirical study on 56 GitHub OSS projects that use DVC to understand the DVC usage pattern and the impact of using DVC on the software development process. We found that Versioning and tracking is the most adopted DVC feature, being utilized by all 56 projects and being the only adopted feature in 85.7% of them. Furthermore, we found that DVC has a significant impact on the software development process indicators such as the number of created pull requests (PRs), and the number of bug-fix commits. For instance, our findings showed that DVC causes a peak in the number of commits and PRs at the moment of the adoption, followed by a long-term decrease. We believe that our findings can assist practitioners in tailoring tools to better meet user requirements and help organizations realize potential outcomes of adopting such tools.

sample_claims.text: The training dataset's lineage is traceable from the original data sources through every preprocessing step to the trained model
The dataset version and pipeline configuration behind any prior release of the credit-scoring model are recorded in version control and can be restored for inspection
All modifications to sensor calibration data and feature extraction steps are documented with timestamps and author attribution
Each release of the defect-detection model is tagged in version control with the record of the training data and pipeline settings that produced it
Every committed change to the training data since the model was first approved can be listed, with date and author, from the project's version history before each new release is signed off
